Thanks Kyle — got the telemetry and good set of signals. Quick clarifying questions so our estimate isn’t wildly off:

1) Prompt/response token distribution: can you share median & 95th for both? If you don’t have exact histograms, rough buckets (e.g., 70% prompts <64 tokens, 20% 64–512, 10% >512) are fine.
2) Session affinity / KV cache reuse: do you pin sessions to GPUs or is each request independent? Any info on average session TTL helps with KV cache hit-rate assumptions.
3) Acceptable fallback policy: if Dedicated is saturated, do you prefer queued requests, degraded models (smaller quantized variant), or regional fallback? This affects the SLA curve we present.
4) Peak burst characteristics: how long are 95th-percentile bursts (seconds/minutes/hours)?

I’ve looped in Marissa (Solutions Architect) — she’ll sketch a GPU-concurrency mapping and a sensitivity table. I’ll produce a short matrix PDF for your execs once we have the above.

Proposed next step: 30-min sync tomorrow to review assumptions and draft. Does 10:00 PT work?

Kyle / Tessa —

I pulled a rough first-pass mapping based on the sample you sent and some conservative assumptions:

- Assumptions used: 8k token context max, mixed-precision quantized model variant for fallbacks, KV cache reuse of ~12% (session affinity moderate).
- Rough throughput mapping (A100-equivalent baseline, 16GB perf-class):
  * 8 GPUs -> ~350 concurrent short-chat sessions (avg 40 tokens response) or ~120 concurrent code-gen sessions (avg 400 tokens response)
  * 16 GPUs -> ~720 concurrent short-chat / ~250 code-gen
  * 32 GPUs -> ~1.4k short-chat / ~520 code-gen

- SLA sensitivity notes: moving p99 tail target from 50ms -> 150ms allows batching/aggregation that reduces GPU cost by ~18–28% for steady-state traffic but provides only modest gain for very short bursts (under ~30s). For multi-minute sustained bursts the savings are larger because batching and prefetch windows are more effective.

I’ve attached a quick workbook (workload_mapping_v1.xlsx) that enumerates these numbers and shows token assumptions per workload profile. To tighten this we’ll need: token histograms, per-endpoint concurrency by time-of-day, and a short list of high-cost prompts (top 1% by tokens).

If you’re ok I’ll convert this into a 1-page executive matrix and call out recommendation for a canary (16 GPUs for 2 weeks) and an autoscale burst pool size.

—Marissa
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Attachments: workload_mapping_v1.xlsx

Tessa / Marissa —

Thanks for the quick turnaround. Answers inline below.

> 1) Prompt/response token distribution
>
We pulled the histograms you asked for (summarized):
- Prompts: median 28 tokens, 95th 420 tokens. Buckets: 78% <64, 15% 64–512, 7% >512.
- Responses: median 86 tokens, 95th 1,200 tokens. Buckets: 60% <128, 25% 128–1024, 15% >1024.

> 2) Session affinity / KV cache reuse
>
We maintain session affinity for authenticated users; estimated KV reuse ~18% for chat flows, lower for code-gen routes (~6%). Average session TTL ~8 minutes.

> 3) Acceptable fallback
>
Prefer degraded-model fallback (quantized smaller variant) for burst overflow over cross-region because we’re sensitive to data locality. Queueing acceptable for non-interactive endpoints only.

> 4) Burst characteristics
>
95th bursts typically last 4–6 minutes; rare incidents (e.g., product launches) can sustain 30–90 minutes. Peak bursts are spiky: median inter-arrival within burst ~120ms.

We uploaded a slightly larger telemetry sample to the Drive link in case you need more granularity. Happy to take the 10:00 PT sync tomorrow.

—Kyle
